title: Planck and Blackbody Radiation
short: Planck's quantized energies explain the blackbody spectrum, and Wien's and Stefan's laws follow from it.
trouble: Students think the ultraviolet catastrophe was something measured, rather than a failed prediction of classical physics.

blocks.html: In Physics 2 you used two rules for glowing objects: hotter objects radiate much more ($P = \sigma AT^4$) and peak at shorter wavelengths ($\lambda_{\max}T = 2.898 \times 10^{-3}$ m·K). Around 1900 these were measured facts that classical physics could not explain. Max Planck's fix, energy that comes only in lumps of $hf$, was the first step into quantum physics, and it also explains the photon.

Planck assumed that the energy of radiation at frequency $f$ can change only in steps of $hf$. Then each mode of radiation in a hot cavity holds, on average, $$\langle E\rangle = \frac{hf}{e^{hf/k_BT} - 1}$$ instead of the classical $k_BT$. This gives the blackbody spectrum $$I(\lambda, T) = \frac{2\pi hc^2}{\lambda^5}\,\frac{1}{e^{hc/\lambda k_BT} - 1},$$ which peaks at $\lambda_{\max} = \frac{2.898 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m·K}}{T}$ (Wien) and has total power $\sigma T^4$ per square meter (Stefan–Boltzmann).

Classical physics gives every mode of the radiation in a hot box the same average energy, $k_BT$. But the number of modes per wavelength interval grows like $1/\lambda^4$ as the wavelength shrinks, so the predicted energy grows without limit toward the ultraviolet: the Rayleigh–Jeans law, which works at long wavelengths and fails badly at short ones. Planck's steps change the average. A mode can hold $0, hf, 2hf, \ldots$, each with Boltzmann weight $e^{-nhf/k_BT}$. Averaging, $$\langle E\rangle = \frac{\sum_n nhf\,e^{-nhf/k_BT}}{\sum_n e^{-nhf/k_BT}} = \frac{hf}{e^{hf/k_BT} - 1}.$$ When $hf \ll k_BT$ this is close to $k_BT$, the classical value. When $hf \gg k_BT$ even one step costs too much, the weight $e^{-hf/k_BT}$ is tiny, and the mode is nearly empty. High frequencies are frozen out, and the spectrum turns down.

blocks.cap: Planck curves for the Sun's surface (5772 K) and a cooler star (3500 K), with the classical Rayleigh–Jeans prediction for the first. The classical curve matches at long wavelengths and shoots upward at short ones.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Average energy per mode, in units of $k_BT$. Classical physics says 1 for every mode. Planck's steps agree for small $hf/k_BT$ and fall off fast once a single step $hf$ is several times $k_BT$.

blocks.title: The Sun's peak
blocks.q: The Sun's surface is at about 5772 K. Where does its spectrum peak?
blocks.a: About 502 nm, blue-green light (the Sun still looks white because it emits strongly at all visible wavelengths)

blocks.title: You glow too
blocks.q: Skin is at about 306 K. At what wavelength does it radiate most strongly?
blocks.a: About 9.5 μm, in the infrared, which is what thermal cameras see

blocks.title: A frozen-out mode
blocks.q: At $T = 5000$ K, compare the average energy of a mode of wavelength 500 nm with the classical $k_BT$. ($hc = 1240$ eV·nm, $k_B = 8.617 \times 10^{-5}$ eV/K.)
blocks.a: Under 2% of the classical value: the steps are too big for the heat to fill

blocks.html: Thinking the “ultraviolet catastrophe” was something measured. It was a prediction of classical physics: infinite energy in the short-wavelength radiation of any warm object. Experiments showed the opposite, a spectrum that turns down and goes to zero at short wavelengths. The failed prediction (named later, in 1911) is what pointed to quantized energy.
Using $\lambda_{\max}T$ with the temperature in degrees Celsius. Wien's law needs kelvins: a 25 °C room is 298 K.
